records.value: (a) Speed is how fast a body moves: speed = distance / time. Velocity = displacement / time. You find how far the body has changed position in a straight line, in a stated direction, and divide by the time taken. Speed uses total distance (a scalar), but velocity uses displacement and direction (a vector), and the direction is shown by the sign. A speedometer shows speed only. (b) Car A: v = 150 m / 7.5 s = 20 m/s towards Nakuru, so +20 m/s. (c) Divide km/h by 3.6: 72 / 3.6 = 20 m/s and 108 / 3.6 = 30 m/s. (d) Oncoming lorry L: its speed is 150 m / 7.5 s = 20 m/s. It travels towards Naivasha, opposite to the positive direction (towards Nakuru), so its velocity is -20 m/s. The negative sign shows direction, not slowing down. (e) Car A's graph is a straight line from (0 s, 0 m) to (7.5 s, 150 m); its gradient is 150/7.5 = +20 m/s. Lorry L's graph is a straight line from (0 s, 0 m) to (7.5 s, -150 m); its gradient is -150/7.5 = -20 m/s, and the downward slope shows motion towards Naivasha. A flat line would show rest (velocity 0). (f) The matatu's line runs from (0 min, 0 km) to (60 min, 60 km). The car's line runs from (0 min, 60 km) to (40 min, 0 km), because 60 km at 90 km/h takes 40 min. The lines cross at 24 min and 24 km from Naivasha. Check: matatu 60 x 0.4 = 24 km; car 90 x 0.4 = 36 km; 24 + 36 = 60 km. At the crossing both vehicles are at the same place at the same time. This is a real-life use of a displacement-time graph: finding when and where two travellers meet.

records.new: If asked for numbers, reply: 'Hold that question for Lesson 3; write it on the DQB.' Language support for English learners: write each key word in English with a Kiswahili word beside it, for example distance - umbali, speed - kasi, direction - mwelekeo, time - muda, acceleration - mchapuko. Let learners say the idea in the language they think in first, then use the sentence frames in pairs before speaking to the class. Ask a Kiswahili-teaching colleague to confirm these words and to supply the words for displacement and velocity, which are not fixed here.
records.group_headline: The plan had no language support for English learners; added Kiswahili key words (to be confirmed by a Kiswahili colleague), graph-drawing supports and oral or sketch ways to show understanding.

records.why: Graph drawing is the main task of this lesson and had no accommodation for learners with visual or motor difficulties or for learners who show understanding better in words or movement.
records.old: What does that tell us about the direction of the cyclist's movement?'
records.new: What does that tell us about the direction of the cyclist's movement?' Supports: for learners with low vision or weak fine-motor control, give an enlarged grid with the axes already drawn and the points marked boldly so they only join them; for learners who find choosing a scale hard, start from a pre-marked scale and let them discuss why it fits; any learner may describe or act out the graph aloud before drawing it.

records.why: The culminating task only offered written and gallery-talk routes; guideline 12 asks for more than one way to show understanding.
records.old: 'I claim... The evidence is... This shows that...'
records.new: 'I claim... The evidence is... This shows that...' Learners who find writing hard may give the claim-evidence-reasoning aloud to a partner or to you, or present it as an annotated sketch of their model, and may write first in Kiswahili and then add the key science words in English.

records.why: Guideline 8 asks for materials available in Kenyan partner schools with low-cost substitutes. Lesson 1 depends entirely on a video clip.
records.old: Do NOT give any measured values, split times or formulas.
records.new: Do NOT give any measured values, split times or formulas. If there is no projector or no power, tell the story from four labelled frames drawn on the board or on a printed storyboard (start, B just behind A, B beside A, B back in lane) and act the overtake out with three learners or three objects on a desk; keep the Notice | Wonder table the same.
records.group_headline: The plan relied on a video projector, graph paper and A3 paper; low-cost substitutes are now listed for each.

records.why: Lessons 4 to 10 all use graph paper, which many partner schools lack; this is the first lesson that needs it.
records.old: Remind learners that displacement has direction, as met in Lesson 2.
records.new: Remind learners that displacement has direction, as met in Lesson 2. Low-cost substitute for graph paper (also for Lessons 5 to 10): a ruled 1 cm grid drawn on a page of an exercise book or on manila paper, or squared exercise books; one ruler can be shared by a pair.

records.why: The final model panels are built on A3 paper, which may not be available.
records.old: redirect to Lesson 3 (velocity and acceleration calculations) and Lesson 7 (gradient and area) work.
records.new: redirect to Lesson 3 (velocity and acceleration calculations) and Lesson 7 (gradient and area) work. If A3 paper is not available, use manila paper, flip-chart paper or four joined exercise-book pages with hand-drawn grids.

records.why: Lessons 7 to 10 and the Final Explanation use a 'split-time table' for checking, but the table was never given in the lesson plans, so a teacher who did not write them could not run the check. Values recomputed: B distance = 20t + t^2 up to t = 5 (21, 44, 69, 96, 125), then +30 m per second (155, 185) and 200 m at 7.5 s; A = 20t.
records.old: extend faster learners by asking them to find the area under A's line from 0 to 5 s (100 m) and compare with the table.
records.new: extend faster learners by asking them to find the area under A's line from 0 to 5 s (100 m) and compare with the table. Give each pair the split-time table (also printed in the Final Explanation): t = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7.5 s; B distance = 0, 21, 44, 69, 96, 125, 155, 185, 200 m; A distance = 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, 140, 150 m. A teacher can rebuild B's column from d = 20t + t^2 for t up to 5 s, then add 30 m each second.

records.why: The supporting phenomenon described a 3 km out-and-back boda boda trip (6 km), but the lessons use Juma (3 km east, 1 km back: distance 4 km, displacement 2 km) and the cyclist Atieno (12 km, displacement 0). Rewritten to match what is taught (checked: 3 + 1 = 4; 3 - 1 = 2; 6 + 6 = 12). The matatu, 800 m runner and railway examples are not used in later lessons; teachers may keep them as extra context.
records.old: • A boda boda rider travels 3 km away from a shopping centre and then returns, ending close to the starting point although the distance travelled is 6 km.
records.new:
• A boda boda rider, Juma, rides 3 km east from the Naivasha stage and then 1 km back west, so the distance travelled is 4 km but he ends only 2 km from the stage.
• A cyclist, Atieno, rides 6 km to the Lake Naivasha gate and back home, covering 12 km but ending with displacement 0.

records.why: KICD lists these three PCIs: Learner Support Programmes (Sports and Games), Socio-Economic and Environmental Issues (Safety and Security) and Road safety. The data listed 'Road safety education', 'Citizenship' and 'Safety and security'; 'Citizenship' is not in the KICD list. Names restored; each is tied to an activity in the lessons.
records.value:
• Road safety: learners work out the relative speed of two vehicles when one is overtaking and discuss the dangers of careless overtaking on roads such as the Nairobi-Nakuru highway.
• Socio-Economic and Environmental Issues (Safety and Security): learners observe two bodies in motion, such as cars overtaking or moving in opposite directions, and work out their relative speed.
• Learner Support Programmes (Sports and Games): learners relate velocity and acceleration to races, for example a Kenyan 800 m runner speeding up at the start and sprinting at the finish.
records.reference: KICD Grade 10 curriculum design, Mathematics, Strand 2.0 Measurements and Geometry, Sub-Strand 2.9 Linear Motion

records.why: Level names (Exceeds / Meets / Approaches expectations) now appear in the descriptor text because the printed headings are fixed by the template. Criteria 1 and 2 now cover speed and displacement-time graphs so that every KICD question is assessed, and the safety criterion asks for a limit of the model (matches the new Final Explanation parts and Lesson 9).

value.criterion: Speed, velocity and acceleration methods (KICD Question 1)
value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: states speed = distance/time, velocity = displacement/time and a = (v - u)/t, explains the vector nature and sign of velocity, converts units correctly and calculates A's +20 m/s, the lorry's -20 m/s, B's 2 m/s^2 and the matatu's -2 m/s^2 with units.
value.proficient: Meets expectations: uses the formulas correctly with minor slips in units or in explaining the sign, and gets most values right.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: confuses speed with velocity or omits conversion, the sign or units, and gets several values wrong.

value.criterion: Graphs: displacement-time and velocity-time, gradient and area (KICD Questions 2 and 3)
value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: sketches correct labelled displacement-time graphs (A, L) and velocity-time graphs (A, B), reads velocity from a gradient, finds the meeting point of two vehicles, links the velocity-time gradient to acceleration, and finds B 200 m (125 + 75) and A 150 m from areas, checking against the table.
value.proficient: Meets expectations: draws mostly correct graphs, reads gradients and finds the distances with a small error or without checking against the table.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: graphs are missing labels or shapes are wrong, and the gradient or area is not linked to velocity, acceleration or distance.

value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: subtracts for the same direction (10 m/s, 36 km/h) and adds for opposite directions (50 m/s, 180 km/h), states the viewpoint, notes 0 at t = 0 and explains why A looks slow from B.
value.proficient: Meets expectations: calculates relative speeds correctly but gives limited explanation or omits the viewpoint or the starting value.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: adds or subtracts incorrectly, or cannot explain why A looks slow.

value.criterion: Safety decision and use of data
value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: correctly finds the lorry's 150 m, the 350 m of road used, the 150 m (3.0 s) margin and the unsafe 50 m (1.0 s) case, uses table values accurately and states a limit of the model.
value.proficient: Meets expectations: reaches the correct decision with one calculation error or a missing unit or time conversion.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: decision is not supported by calculations or the numbers are inconsistent with the data.

value.criterion: Final Explanation answering the driving question
value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: connects speed, velocity, acceleration, graphs, relative speed and safety in a clear, logical explanation that uses the Naivasha evidence and answers all three KICD questions.
value.proficient: Meets expectations: answers the driving question using most ideas but with some links missing.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: lists facts without linking them to the overtake or the driving question.

records.why: The current partner contract allows only three rubric level fields (excellent, proficient, developing), so the fourth CBE level, Below Expectations, cannot be represented in the data. Suggested fix: allow a fourth field in the contract, or print a fixed 'Below Expectations' column in the template. Teacher/partner decision needed.

Numbering mismatch against KICD: the KICD Grade 10 Mathematics design lists this as Strand 2.0 Measurements and Geometry, Sub-Strand 2.9 Linear Motion (15 lessons); the data says Strand 3.0 / Sub-Strand 3.4 throughout. Not renamed, as instructed. Please check whether the school's scheme of work (for example a different pathway or order) uses 3.0 / 3.4 deliberately.

records.why: KICD content not taught: the suggested experience 'participate in a race of a specified distance, record the time taken by each learner and work out velocity and acceleration' (and the matching Self-efficacy competency and Sports and Games PCI) has no hands-on activity; all numbers come from the clip and data cards. Suggestion: add an optional timing task in Lesson 3 or as homework, for example learners time a 50 m run with stopwatches or phone timers in the school compound and compute average velocity and the acceleration over the first 10 m, away from any road. Needs a teacher decision because it adds equipment and outdoor time.
